claims.text: The baseline [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69 alloy is a homogeneous, disordered BCC solid solution.
The baseline Ti-rich Ta-Nb-Ti-Zr-Hf alloy exhibits robust superconductivity and a zero-resistance state.
Superconductivity in the baseline [TaNb]0.31(TiZrHf)0.69 alloy is phonon-mediated.
Approximately 10 atomic percent of Zr will be replaced by U while retaining the other constituents.
The modified alloy is intended to remain a single-phase BCC solid solution with every element at or above 5 atomic percent.
Random atomic-scale chemical disorder in the BCC lattice sets the local electronic environment and density of states near the Fermi level.
An optimal average valence electron count enhances the density of states and electron-phonon coupling needed for superconductivity.
Replacing Zr with U can preserve a similar overall electron count.
U introduces localized spin-orbit effects or fluctuating magnetic moments, potentially even in an intermediate-valence state.
The proposed localized U-related effects break Cooper pairs.
U-related pair breaking reduces Tc even when the overall electron count is maintained.
Relative to the baseline, the approximately 10 atomic percent U-substituted alloy should have a measurably lower Tc.
The U-substituted alloy may have a lower upper critical field Hc2 than the baseline.
The reported U-containing [TaNb]0.31(TiUHf)0.69 alloy is BCC and phonon-mediated, with Tc approximately 3.2 K and Hc2 approximately 6.4 T.
A Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr-Ti BCC HEA retains zero-resistance superconductivity under pressures up to approximately 190.6 GPa without a structural phase transition.
The proposed mechanism applies only while the alloy remains a homogeneous BCC solid solution without secondary phases or ordering and while electron-phonon coupling remains dominant.
Tc and Hc2 can be compared using resistivity, magnetic susceptibility, and field-dependent transport or magnetization, with X-ray diffraction used to verify the phase.
Tc and Hc2 statistically equivalent to or higher than the baseline would falsify the proposed U-induced pair-breaking hypothesis.
